doc: Inferring where the buses are along a route from nothing but each stop's soonest arrival (ADR-030). No vehicle ids exist in HK open data, so the rule is a discontinuity scan: going forward, one bus reaches successive stops at increasing times, therefore a stop whose soonest arrival is SOONER than its predecessor's (or whose predecessor shows nothing) is being approached by a DIFFERENT bus — the lead bus has already left the earlier stop, which now shows the one behind it. Each such discontinuity is one marker. `atStop` is true only when that arrival is imminent (< 1 min), in which case the marker is drawn ON the stop node; otherwise it is drawn at the midpoint of the segment leading into it. We never interpolate a position from a clock — the marker moves only when fresh ETA data arrives (ADR-008). `soonest[i]` is the ISO arrival at stop i or JSON null for none; ISO strings carry a fixed +08:00 offset, so lexical comparison is chronological and a port must NOT need to parse them to order them.

inferBusMarkers.doc: Ordered markers, one per inferred bus, ascending by `toIndex`. `toIndex` is the stop the bus is heading TO (its next stop, by array position).

cases.note: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW. One second under two minutes, at the first stop. The marker is off the node (`atStop` false) and sits on the approach segment. The point of pinning all three of 119/120/121 here: the LABEL changes across this boundary ('1 min' -> '2 min') while the MARKER does not move at all. A port that derived `atStop` from the rendered minutes — or that recomputed the marker whenever the label changed — would either jitter the bus or park it on the node. `atStop` is a function of seconds, never of the displayed minute.
NAMED BOUNDARY ROW. Exactly two minutes. Identical marker to the 119 s row.
NAMED BOUNDARY ROW. One second past two minutes. Still identical.
59 s. The only condition that sets `atStop`, and it is the same < 60 s window that makes the label read 'Due'.
60 s. The first second the marker leaves the node.
Increasing times all the way along means a single bus, marked at the first stop only. Three arrivals, ONE marker — the row that catches a port drawing a bus per stop with an ETA.

12:02, 12:05, then 12:01 — the drop at index 2 cannot be the same bus, so a second one is heading there. Index 3's 12:09 is later than index 2's 12:01, so it is that same second bus and gets no marker of its own.
Most stops on a long route have no live reading at all, so this is the common shape, not an edge case. A null predecessor means 'nothing known behind me', which the rule treats as a discontinuity.
The comparison is strictly `prev > a`, so equal readings do NOT count as a discontinuity. Two adjacent stops reporting the same second is a feed artefact, not two buses.
Beyond the -60 s tolerance the reading is stale rubbish, so no bus is drawn for it.

DEFECT, and the one worth reading twice. Stop 0 shows 12:00 minus 2 min (the bus has gone; its reading has not refreshed) and stop 1 shows 12:01. Stop 0 is dropped as departed. Stop 1 is then judged NOT a lead, because its predecessor's time (11:58) is EARLIER than its own — the discontinuity test never learns that the predecessor was discarded. Result: no marker anywhere, and a bus that is genuinely one minute from stop 1 vanishes from the route view. The departed check and the lead check disagree about which readings exist. Fix: drop departed readings BEFORE the discontinuity scan, so a departed predecessor counts as absent. Recorded as-is so every platform agrees while it stands; when it is fixed, `expect` becomes [{ toIndex: 1, atStop: false }] and all suites go red until ported.
30 s in the past is inside the +/-60 s window, so it is 'Due', not departed, and the marker sits ON the stop. The tolerance band exists for feed clock skew and this proves the marker honours it too.
The normal state of a route late at night. Empty, not an error.
